lead: A column carries load mainly in compression. Its behaviour changes if it can bend sideways between its ends. Two ideas decide that behaviour: how the ends are restrained, which gives the effective length, and how thin the column is, which gives the slenderness ratio. Together they sort a column into short or slender. Short columns are designed for axial load plus a small minimum eccentricity; slender columns need extra moments. This classification comes first in every column design, before steel is chosen in 5.2 or moments are checked in 5.3.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for limit state philosophy and material behaviour, and the bending picture of Unit 2.

sections.h3: Tied and spiral columns; braced and unbraced frames

blocks.text: A column is a vertical compression member. Two independent groupings matter before any steel is designed. The first is how the longitudinal bars are held: by ties or by a spiral. The second is how the frame resists sideways movement: braced or unbraced.

A tied column has vertical bars and separate lateral ties. A tie is a closed loop of small diameter bar, spaced along the height. Ties hold the bars in position and stop them buckling outward. Most building columns are tied columns.

A spiral column has one continuous helical spiral in place of ties. The spiral confines the concrete core. A confined core carries more load and deforms more before failure, so spiral columns are used in bridge piers and heavy industrial work. The design formulas differ, but the classification in this chapter is the same.

A braced column belongs to a frame with a lateral support system — shear walls, bracing or a stiff core — so the frame cannot sway. An unbraced column relies on its own frame action to resist sway. Braced frames give smaller effective lengths. Unbraced frames give larger ones. The same section can be short in a braced frame and slender in an unbraced frame.

The clear height between supports is the unsupported length l. It is not the length that controls buckling. A fixed end resists rotation; a pinned end does not. The effective length is l_eff = K l, where K is the effective length factor and l is the unsupported length.

For a braced frame, K is usually between 0.65 and 1.0. For an unbraced frame, K is greater than 1.0. Use the value from the frame analysis or the code table for the actual end restraints; the four values above are the standard ideal cases.

The slenderness ratio about an axis is λ = l_eff / d. Here l_eff is the effective length about that axis and d is the lateral dimension perpendicular to that axis. For a rectangular section b × D, bending about the major axis has d = D; bending about the minor axis has d = b. Check both axes.

blocks.where: λ is the slenderness ratio (dimensionless); l_eff is the effective length about the axis, in mm; d is the lateral dimension perpendicular to that axis, in mm.

blocks.text: A column is short when both ratios are less than 12. It is slender when either ratio is 12 or more. The number 12 is a design line. Below it, the sideways deflection under load adds a second-order moment small enough to neglect. At or above it, that extra moment must be added, and the column is designed as slender. Some syllabi call the slenderness ratio the column slenderness.

Even a short column is not loaded perfectly axially. Construction tolerances and accidental load positions give a minimum eccentricity: e_min = l/500 + D/30, and not less than 20 mm. l is the unsupported length in mm. D is the lateral dimension in the direction of bending, in mm. e_min is in mm. The 20 mm floor prevents an unrealistically small design moment. Use the larger of the calculated value and 20 mm.

blocks.where: e_min is the minimum eccentricity in mm; l is the unsupported length in mm; D is the lateral dimension in the direction of bending in mm; max( , ) takes the larger value.

figure.caption: The route from a column to its effective length and then to the two slenderness ratios. In the worked example the ratios are 8.0 and 12.0, so the minor ratio is not less than 12 and the column is slender (borderline).

spec.title: Column classification
spec.aria: Flow from column to effective length to slenderness ratios, then to short if both ratios are less than 12 or slender if any ratio is 12 or more.

examples.question: A tied column has section b × D = 300 mm × 450 mm and unsupported length 3.6 m. Both ends are pinned in a braced frame. Find the effective length, the slenderness ratios about both axes, the minimum eccentricity about each axis, and classify the column as short or slender.
steps: Both ends pinned gives K = 1.0. The unsupported length is l = 3.6 m = 3600 mm. The effective length is l_eff = K l = 1.0 × 3600 = 3600 mm = 3.6 m.
About the major axis, the lateral dimension is D = 450 mm. The slenderness ratio is λ_major = l_eff / D = 3600 / 450 = 8.0.
About the minor axis, the lateral dimension is b = 300 mm. The slenderness ratio is λ_minor = l_eff / b = 3600 / 300 = 12.0.
λ_minor = 12.0 is not less than 12, so the column is slender (borderline).
Minimum eccentricity about the minor axis, lateral dimension in the direction of bending = b = 300 mm: e_min = 3600/500 + 300/30 = 7.2 + 10 = 17.2 mm. The floor is 20 mm, so e_min = 20.0 mm.

Minimum eccentricity about the major axis, lateral dimension in the direction of bending = D = 450 mm: e_min = 3600/500 + 450/30 = 7.2 + 15 = 22.2 mm. This is above the floor, so e_min = 22.2 mm. The e_min formula takes the section dimension in the direction of bending, whichever axis is being checked.
examples.answer: Effective length = 3.6 m; slenderness ratios = 8.0 and 12.0; minimum eccentricities = 20.0 mm and 22.2 mm; the column is slender (borderline).
examples.check:
l = 3600.0
K = 1.0
L_eff = K * l
lam_major = L_eff / 450.0
lam_minor = L_eff / 300.0
e_min_minor = max(20.0, L_eff/500.0 + 300.0/30.0)
e_min_major = max(20.0, L_eff/500.0 + 450.0/30.0)
print(f"{L_eff/1000:.1f}")
print(f"{lam_major:.1f}")
print(f"{lam_minor:.1f}")
print(f"{e_min_minor:.1f}")
print(f"{e_min_major:.1f}")

traps: Using the unsupported length l in place of l_eff. The 12 limit applies to λ = l_eff / d, not to the clear height.
Checking only the major axis. The minor axis often has the larger ratio because its lateral dimension d is smaller.
Putting the wrong dimension in the denominator. For each axis, use the section dimension perpendicular to that axis; do not use the least lateral dimension for both axes.
Forgetting the 20 mm floor. l/500 + D/30 can come out below 20 mm, and then 20 mm governs.
Treating a spiral column automatically as slender. Ties and spirals describe construction; short or slender comes from the slenderness ratios.

quiz.q: Define the effective length of a column.
quiz.a: It is l_eff = K l, where l is the unsupported length and K is the effective length factor set by the end restraints. It is the length used for buckling and slenderness.

quiz.q: State the limit that separates a short column from a slender column.
quiz.a: Both slenderness ratios < 12 means short. Any one ratio ≥ 12 means slender.

quiz.q: Why is the effective length used instead of the clear height when computing slenderness?
quiz.a: Buckling depends on how the ends are held. A fixed end resists rotation and reduces the length that can buckle. K l represents that buckling length, so it gives the correct slenderness.

quiz.q: Why does a nominally axial column need a minimum eccentricity?
quiz.a: Construction tolerances and accidental load positions create small moments. The minimum eccentricity sets a floor so the design is not based on a perfect axial load that never occurs.

quiz.q: A braced column is 4.0 m unsupported with both ends fixed. Its section is 250 mm × 400 mm. Find both slenderness ratios and classify it.
quiz.a: Both ends fixed gives K = 0.65, so l_eff = 0.65 × 4000 = 2600 mm. Major axis: 2600 / 400 = 6.5. Minor axis: 2600 / 250 = 10.4. Both are < 12, so the column is short.

quiz.q: For a 300 mm × 300 mm column with unsupported length 2.4 m, find e_min.
A column is 300 mm × 600 mm with l_eff = 4.2 m. One student says it is short because 4200/600 = 7.0 < 12. Is the student right?
quiz.a: No. The minor axis must also be checked: 4200/300 = 14.0 ≥ 12. The column is slender.

quiz.q: Explain why the same column can be short in a braced frame and slender in an unbraced frame.
quiz.a: An unbraced frame gives a larger K, hence a larger l_eff. The ratios l_eff/d rise and may reach 12 or more, even when the section and clear height are unchanged.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, column effective lengths come from a frame analysis that includes the stiffness of beams at each joint, not from a single K table. Modern software builds the frame, applies second-order effects directly, and checks both axes together. Research on confined concrete uses spiral and hoop details to improve ductility in seismic zones. Search for 'effective length factor braced unbraced frame', 'second-order effects RC column', and 'confinement spiral column ductility'.
